about: Recorded demo data for Module 3, steps 3.2 and 3.3 (MGMT 615, fictional). 'chosen' is the scenario the demo faculty member keeps; 'alternative' is the second option the AI offers. CLO numbers follow the revised CLOs from step 1.4.
storylinePremise: MGMT 615 is a story about Dana Ortiz, a newly promoted operations manager, who struggles to find and fix the real causes of her site's slipping performance before peak season, when her director has already decided who to blame.

chosen.title: The First Bad Week
chosen.premise: Dana struggles to step back and find out why on-time shipping has dropped, when her instinct is to work extra floor shifts and push the number back up herself.
chosen.situation: Eight months into her first management job, Dana runs a distribution center with three shift leads and about 45 associates. Her job now is to hit site targets through her leads.
chosen.trigger: The Monday report shows on-time shipping down from 97% to 89%, six weeks before peak season. Her director, Greg, has already named the cause: "Jordan's shift is the problem."
chosen.stakeholders: Dana; shift leads Jordan Pike and Ray Kowalski; the hourly crew; Greg; customers waiting on late orders.
chosen.decision: How to spend her week: work the floor to recover the number, accept Greg's read and focus on Jordan, or step back and find out what is driving the drop.
chosen.outcome: Working the floor would lift the number for a few days and hide the cause. Separating a manager's job from a lead's job shows Dana the habit she has carried over. She pulls the error reports instead, which starts the investigation that runs through the course.

alternative.title: The Jammed Sorter
alternative.premise: Dana struggles to decide whether to clear a sorter jam herself or hand it to Jordan, with trucks waiting and the crew watching.

chosen.title: The Bonus That Backfired
chosen.premise: Dana struggles to figure out why a bonus her crew is hitting is making performance worse, and why Luis, one of her most accurate associates, keeps missing it.
chosen.situation: The site pays a pick-rate bonus for speed. The crew is hitting its targets, but on-time shipping keeps falling.
chosen.trigger: Mis-picks and reworked orders are climbing. Luis keeps missing the bonus because he checks the orders others rush.
chosen.stakeholders: Luis and the crew who count on the bonus; Jordan and Ray; Greg; customers.
chosen.decision: Leave the bonus alone and coach for accuracy, add an accuracy threshold, or propose replacing it before peak season.
chosen.outcome: Expectancy theory explains the drop: the crew believes speed earns the reward, so speed is what they deliver. Dana takes Greg a revised bonus tied to accurate, on-time orders, which sets up Module 7.

alternative.title: Luis Checks Out
alternative.premise: Dana struggles to re-engage Luis, passed over for a lead role last spring, when the only reward the site offers is a bonus he refuses to chase.

chosen.title: The Conversation With Jordan
chosen.premise: Dana struggles to run a coaching conversation that changes how Jordan closes out his shift, when her director wants it documented as a formal warning.
chosen.situation: Dana needs Jordan, her day-shift lead, to change how he hands off to night shift. He came up under her and avoids hard conversations with his crew.
chosen.trigger: Orders keep slipping in the hour around shift change, and Jordan has turned defensive. Greg tells Dana to issue a formal warning.
chosen.stakeholders: Jordan; Dana; Greg; Ray, whose shift inherits the unfinished work; the day-shift crew.
chosen.decision: Issue the warning Greg wants, hold a coaching conversation with no record, or coach first and document only the next steps they agree on.
chosen.outcome: A warning would put Jordan on record without changing how he closes out his shift. Separating coaching from discipline lets Dana name one behavior and the change she expects, while keeping a record Greg can see.

alternative.title: The Repeated Shortcut
alternative.premise: Dana struggles to decide whether a repeated safety shortcut on Ray's shift calls for coaching or for discipline.

chosen.title: The Handoff Nobody Owns
chosen.premise: Dana struggles to fix the broken handoff between her two shifts with a structural change, when her director is pushing a team-building lunch.
chosen.situation: The two shifts pass work to each other every afternoon, but no one owns the handoff. Unfinished orders and staffing gaps fall between the leads.
chosen.trigger: Ray and Jordan now blame each other's shifts for the late orders. Greg suggests a team-building lunch to get everyone on the same page.
chosen.stakeholders: Jordan and Ray; both crews; Dana; Greg; customers.
chosen.decision: Host the lunch, hold a joint meeting to air the tension, or change the structure: name a handoff owner and add a shared checklist and an overlap window.
chosen.outcome: A team-effectiveness framework shows the problem is unclear roles and process, so a lunch won't touch it. Dana proposes the structural fix and has to explain to Greg why it beats his idea.

alternative.title: Two Shifts, Two Rulebooks
alternative.premise: Dana struggles to get day and night shift working from one set of procedures, when each lead insists his shift's way is the reason it performs.

chosen.title: Telling Greg He's Wrong
chosen.premise: Dana struggles to disagree with her director, using evidence, before he replaces Jordan for a problem Jordan didn't cause alone.
chosen.situation: Dana has data from Alicia Grant's dashboard showing late orders clustered around shift change on both shifts, and mis-picks rising since the bonus started.
chosen.trigger: Greg emails: "Fix him or replace him. I want a plan by Friday." On a follow-up call he says he doesn't need a study.
chosen.stakeholders: Greg; Jordan, whose job is at risk; Dana, whose credibility is on the line; Ray and Alicia, who favor replacing Jordan; the crew.
chosen.decision: Send the replacement plan, agree to a warning and fix the handoff quietly, or ask for 30 minutes to walk Greg through the data and propose a two-week handoff fix first.
chosen.outcome: Mapping the conflict shows a process problem, which changes what the conversation is about. A structured plan lets Dana open with evidence instead of defending Jordan.

alternative.title: Ray vs. Jordan
alternative.premise: Dana struggles to settle a floor argument between her shift leads that looks personal but is really about a process neither one owns.

chosen.title: Twelve Things on Dana's List
chosen.premise: Dana struggles to decide which of her twelve peak-season responsibilities to keep and which to hand off, after a lead gets an overtime call wrong.
chosen.situation: Peak season has started. Dana has twelve responsibilities, from carrier escalations to overtime approvals, and her first review called her a bottleneck.
chosen.trigger: In the first week of the peak push, her leads miss an overtime rule. Dana's instinct is to take every overtime call back.
chosen.stakeholders: Dana; Jordan and Ray; associates working overtime; Greg; Alicia, who delegates heavily.
chosen.decision: Sort the list into keep, hand off, and hand off with checkpoints. The hardest call is who owns the shift handoff and overtime approvals.
chosen.outcome: A delegation framework helps Dana hand the shift handoff to one lead with a weekly checkpoint and keep overtime approvals for now, with a date to revisit. She has to justify that trade-off to Greg.

alternative.title: The Scheduling Tool Says Cut
alternative.premise: Dana struggles to decide whether to follow an AI scheduling tool's recommendation to cut a shift, with a carrier deadline in two days and no time to check its assumptions.

chosen.title: Ending the Bonus
chosen.premise: Dana struggles to announce a change to the bonus in a way her crew will understand and accept, when the floor already calls it a pay cut.
chosen.situation: Greg has approved Dana's revised bonus, which pays for accurate, on-time orders. It starts next pay period.
chosen.trigger: The crew likes the old bonus, and the fastest pickers earn more under it. Before Dana says anything, she hears people calling it a pay cut.
chosen.stakeholders: The crew; Luis, who stands to gain; Jordan and Ray, who will field questions; Greg; Dana.
chosen.decision: Send a written notice, have her leads announce it at shift start, or meet each shift herself and walk through what changes and why.
chosen.outcome: Naming the likely sources of resistance, such as lost income and distrust of a new manager, tells Dana what her message has to answer. She drafts it in plain language: what changes, when it starts, and how to earn the new bonus.

alternative.title: The Overlap Window
alternative.premise: Dana struggles to introduce a thirty-minute shift overlap that both crews see as unpaid extra work.

chosen.title: Proven vs. Potential
chosen.premise: Dana struggles to choose between an experienced outside candidate and Luis, a high-potential associate, for the new shift-lead role that will own the handoff.
chosen.situation: Dana has approval for a new shift-lead role that owns the handoff between shifts, the permanent fix for the gap that started the story.
chosen.trigger: Two finalists: an outside candidate who has run shift operations elsewhere, and Luis, highly accurate but never a supervisor. Ray backs the outside hire, and the crew is watching to see whether Luis gets a shot.
chosen.stakeholders: Luis; the outside candidate; Ray and Jordan; the crew; Greg.
chosen.decision: Hire the proven candidate, hire Luis, or hire one and build a development path for the other.
chosen.outcome: A structured scorecard tied to skills from earlier modules, like coaching and owning a handoff, keeps Dana from deciding on experience or loyalty alone. Whichever she picks, she has to justify the trade-off.

alternative.title: Twenty Temps in Ten Days
alternative.premise: Dana struggles to hire twenty seasonal associates in ten days without falling back on gut feel.
